item.title: Shortening a scale without breaking it
item.dc:creator: Anthony W. Raborn
item.description:
The problem

A long questionnaire costs respondents time, and tired respondents give worse answers. The usual fix is a short form: a subset of the items that measures the same thing.

Picking that subset by hand is hard. The short form has to keep the structure of the full scale, stay reliable, and still relate to outside variables the way the full scale does. Dropping the items with the weakest statistics one at a time tends to satisfy one of those goals at the expense of the others. With 30 items and a target of 10, there are about 30 million possible short forms, so checking them all is not practical either.

What I did

One of my graduate school advisors, Walter Leite, had code from an earlier publication that used an ant colony optimization algorithm to search for good short forms. I turned that code into the ShortForm R package, and we described it in Applied Psychological Measurement in 2018.

The algorithm builds many candidate short forms, fits a model to each one, and makes the items from the better-fitting candidates more likely to be chosen in the next round. It stops when the search keeps returning the same items.

I then added more search methods to the package, including a Tabu search and a new implementation of simulated annealing. With Walter Leite and George Marcoulides, I ran a Monte Carlo simulation comparing four algorithms: ant colony optimization, Tabu search, a genetic algorithm, and simulated annealing. We tested them on scales with one factor, several factors, and a bifactor structure, with and without a misspecified model and an outside variable.

What came out of it

The comparison was published in Educational and Psychological Measurement in 2020. The main findings were:

  • When the model for the full scale was right, or only slightly wrong, all four algorithms produced short forms with good psychometric qualities that kept the structure of the full scale.
  • When the model was badly wrong, every algorithm did worse.
  • Simulated annealing performed best overall and held up best when the model was wrong.
  • The genetic algorithm produced worse-fitting short forms than the others when the model was wrong.

ShortForm is on CRAN, and I have maintained it since 2017. ShinyShortForm puts the same methods behind a web page for people who do not write R.

Where this applies

This is useful if you have a validated instrument that is too long for the setting you need it in, such as a screener, a repeated survey, or one section of a longer battery. You need response data on the full scale and a model of how its items relate.

Sources

Raborn & Leite (2018). ShortForm: An R package to select scale short forms with the ant colony optimization algorithm. Applied Psychological Measurement.

Raborn, Leite & Marcoulides (2020). A comparison of metaheuristic optimization algorithms for scale short-form development. Educational and Psychological Measurement.

ShortForm on CRAN

item.title: Validating a fatigue questionnaire in a phase 3 trial
item.dc:creator: Anthony W. Raborn
item.description:
The problem

Fatigue is one of the symptoms that people with generalized myasthenia gravis (gMG) report. A clinical trial can only use a questionnaire to measure it if there is evidence that the scores mean what they are supposed to mean in that group of patients.

The Neuro-QoL Fatigue is an existing patient-reported measure with a 19-item version and a short form. The question was whether its scores hold up in adults with gMG, and how large a change in a person’s score counts as a real improvement.

What I did

I was first author on the psychometric analysis, working with five coauthors. The data came from Vivacity-MG3, a double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with 196 participants. We used the baseline data and the 24-week double-blind phase.

For both the 19-item version and the short form, we examined:

  • Structure: factor analysis to check that the items measure a single thing.
  • Reliability: internal consistency, and test-retest reliability among participants whose condition was stable.
  • Relationships with other measures: whether scores correlated with related measures and not with unrelated ones.
  • Known groups: whether scores separated groups of patients who differ clinically.
  • Sensitivity to change: whether scores moved when other measures of the patient’s condition moved.
  • Meaningful change: the size of a within-person score change that represents a real improvement.

What came out of it

The results were published in Quality of Life Research in 2025. For the 19-item version:

Evidence Result
Single-factor model fit TLI = 0.99, RMSEA = 0.07
Internal consistency alpha = 0.95
Test-retest reliability, stable participants r = 0.92
Meaningful improvement, 19-item score change of 6.7
Meaningful improvement, short-form score change of 7.6

The short form gave similar results on structure and reliability. Scores from both versions related to other measures as expected, separated clinically distinct groups, and tracked change in other measures. The paper concludes that the evidence supports using Neuro-QoL Fatigue scores to assess fatigue in adults with gMG.

Where this applies

This is useful if you are using a patient-reported measure in a population it was not originally validated in, or if you need a defensible threshold for meaningful change to interpret trial results.

Source

Raborn et al. (2025). Psychometric analysis of the Neuro-QoL Fatigue in generalized myasthenia gravis using data from a phase 3 trial. Quality of Life Research.

item.title: Checking test questions for fairness to small groups
item.dc:creator: Anthony W. Raborn
item.description:
The problem

A test question shows differential item functioning (DIF) when people of the same ability have different chances of answering it correctly depending on which group they belong to. Testing programs screen for DIF so that a question does not count against a group for reasons unrelated to what the test measures.

The standard checks have two limits. They usually compare one focal group with one reference group, which does not suit a variable with many categories. They also need large samples, so the smallest groups, which are often the ones a program most wants to check, get combined with others or skipped.

What I did

I worked with Corinne Huggins-Manley, Peggy Jones and Ted Myers on a nonparametric index called the root expected proportion squared difference, or REPSD. It differs from the standard checks in two ways:

  • It compares each focal group directly with the composite group, meaning everyone whose responses are used to build the reported score scale.
  • It judges statistical significance with Monte Carlo permutations, so it does not need the sample sizes that the standard checks do.

I wrote and maintain the repsd R package that implements it. You give it a matrix of item responses and a column that says who is in the focal group. It returns the REPSD value for each item, a simulated null distribution, and the p-values that flag items for review.

What came out of it

The method was published in the Journal of Educational Measurement in 2024. The paper includes a simulation study of the conditions under which the index gives acceptable Type I error and power, and an application to a school district assessment.

The package is free and on CRAN. A version for items scored in more than two categories is in progress with a student of my PhD advisor.

Where this applies

This is useful if your program reports results for groups that are a small share of test takers, or if the grouping variable you care about has many categories.

Sources

Huggins-Manley, Raborn, et al. (2024). A nonparametric composite group DIF index for focal groups stemming from multicategorical variables. Journal of Educational Measurement.

repsd on CRAN

item.title: Shiny Short Form
item.dc:creator: Anthony W. Raborn
item.description:
ShinyShortForm is a small app demonstrating the ShortForm package. It allows users to modify some of the parameters of the metaheuristic algorithms included in the package and see first-hand how they affect the runtime and output using simulated sample data.

As seen in this screenshot, the app provides the modifiable parameters on the lefthand side of the screen, as well as algorithm-specific information and output on the righthand side of the screen. For each of the algorithms (Ant Colony Optimization, Simulated Annealing, and Tabu Search), the parameter list automatically updates, as well as the manual page. You can press the “Run Selected Algorithm” button to use the default parameters, which result in a (relatively) quick run for each algorithm.

Each algorithm additionally has its own outputs and diagnostic plots that auto-populate after the algorithm has completed its run. The plots allow you to visually inspect how the algorithm searched for its proposed solution. If you modify the parameters, you can easily see how the search changes by keeping an eye on these diagnostic plots across runs.

Note that only a select set of parameters are modifiable on the app and there are restrictions on the values you can input for each parameter. However, you can still end up in a situation where the algorithm takes a long time to find a solution–that’s expected! As long as the Algorithm Output is showing the ASCII animation, the application is working and you can expect a solution eventually.

Have any questions, comments, or ideas? Reach out and let me know!
